messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 61-year-old South Asian man and non-profit worker, has been struggling since a life-threatening motor vehicle collision three months ago. The accident left Ravi with persistent symptoms that have significantly disrupted his daily life. Ravi’s trauma is deeply embedded in the tactile memory of the texture associated with the event; he often feels an overwhelming sense of dread when he encounters similar textures. The incident itself was harrowing: a sudden, loud screech of tires followed by the violent impact of metal against metal. As he sat helplessly in his car, Ravi felt the world closing in on him, and the texture of the seat belt’s fabric seared into his memory. Even now, the tactile sensation of anything similar triggers an immediate flashback, transporting him back to that moment. Ravi’s wife has noticed how often he becomes visibly shaken when they discuss traffic accidents or hear news reports about collisions. The mere mention of such events can bring back the intense fear and terror he experienced during the crash. He frequently starts to sweat and his heart races as if he were reliving the event right then and there. One day at work, Ravi was reading an article about a car accident when the words on the page suddenly transformed into vivid images of his own collision. The sound of a colleague’s footsteps approaching startled him sharply, causing his heart to pound and his breath to catch in his throat as if he were under immediate threat again. In his daily life, Ravi is always on high alert for unexpected or loud sounds, certain that any sudden noise could trigger another terrifying flashback. This hyper-vigilance has made it difficult for him to feel safe in public places like the office where he works. His colleagues have observed how quickly he reacts to even minor movements nearby, often standing up abruptly as if ready to flee. The memory of the event itself is vivid and intrusive. Ravi describes seeing flashes of the scene whenever he closes his eyes or when something triggers a similar sensation. The images are so real that it feels like the crash is happening again, causing him immense distress. Ravi’s work environment has become a source of significant anxiety as well. A recent project required frequent discussions about transportation safety measures, which were particularly triggering for Ravi. He found himself leaving meetings abruptly and avoiding interactions that could lead to these discussions. His colleagues noticed his absence from important conversations and began to question why he seemed so distant. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has taken a toll on Ravi’s personal relationships as well. While his wife is supportive, she also feels concerned about the impact of his behavior on their daily life together. The constant threat of reliving the traumatic event and the fear of encountering similar textures or sounds have made it difficult for Ravi to engage in simple activities he once enjoyed. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a particularly severe episode during which he experienced a full flashback while driving home from work. The intensity of the memory left him feeling disoriented and unsafe, and he realized that his quality of life was deteriorating rapidly. He is most afraid of losing control and having another accident. At the same time, Ravi hopes to regain a sense of normalcy and peace in his daily activities without being constantly haunted by the memories of his traumatic experience.
